speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands) moved:
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
That this House profoundly regrets the two-year delay of the Government in bringing in promised legislation to improve guaranteed income supplements for low-income single elderly Canadians, and condemns the Government for its failure to respond to the innovative proposals of the all-party Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform to expand opportunities for Canadians under age 65 to make adequate provision for income in their retirement years.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the Opposition is able to raise this question of pension reform once again for debate in this House of Commons. We do so in the hope and expectation that somehow it will move the Government forward, if only slightly, to the very real changes which are needed in the pension system in Canada; to make sure that those who are now in greatest need will have their wants addressed; and that there will be changes so that the poverty we see now all too often among our elderly citizens is not perpetuated into the future.
Back in March of 1983, Mr. Speaker, at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, I posed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) concerning the tragic plight in which so many of our elderly citizens find themselves as a result of inadequate income. I asked her when there might be an increase in the guaranteed income supplement so as to relieve their poverty. The Minister responded in this way. Mind you, this was back in March of 1983. She said that "the cost of bringing the single pensioners over the poverty line . . . has been approved by the Government as their first social spending-whenever we can afford it".
[DOT]	(mo)
When I posed that question one year ago, Mr. Speaker, it was not the first time it was asked. It was not the last time that it was posed to the Minister, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Each time they were asked about Canada's elderly poor, the Ministers replied that the needs of this group were their top priority and
that legislation to improve their lot would be the first piece of social legislation which would be brought before the House.
Since then the Minister of National Health and Welfare has seen fit to bring in the Canada Health Act. The Government has introduced measures to put restrictions on transfers for post-secondary education. There have been these Bills and others dealing with social issues, but there is still no sign of legislation to address the pressing needs of Canada's 600,000 elderly poor, the group which the Government has said time and again is their top priority.
The fact that we have 600,000 elderly Canadians living in poverty in a country as rich and bountiful as Canada, in a society supposedly as compassionate and humane as ours, is a national disgrace. The fact that this has been allowed to continue month after month, year after year, is a telling indictment of the Government. The Government is bereft of ideas, drained of decency, and unable to recognize the priorities which must be dealt with in this society. I know the Government has its priorities: bail-outs of de Havilland, Cana-dair and Maislin; bonuses for executive officers in de Havilland and the Canada Development Investment Corporation; and the purchase of Petrofina gas stations. We know what the priorities of the Government are. For the people who have, throughout their lifetimes, worked for and contributed to the development of this great country, there is only a promise trotted out time and time again that some day, some time, they too will become a priority.
Is it any wonder, Sir, that today we condemn the Government? We condemn it not only for its failure to introduce legislation that would meet the current needs of today's elderly poor, but also for its failure to bring about long overdue pension reform of the whole system so that we can ensure that the poverty of today will not be meted out to those who will be senior citizens in 10, 20 or 30 years' time. We must begin to come to grips with this issue and reverse what is happening.
Studies, conferences and task forces on pension reform have been going on for years, Mr. Speaker. It would take the rest of my allotted time today to even name all of the conferences and commissions which have taken place, let alone comment on the recommendations which they have put forward. It was the concern about the difficulties encountered by many of today's elderly, and the prospect of even greater numbers being in straitened circumstances in the not too distant future unless corrective measures are taken quickly, that precipitated most of the studies which have taken place. It was the same concern which precipitated the establishment of the all-Party parliamentary task force on pension reform. I want to pay credit to the work of that task force because it worked long and hard

and studied the issues. I believe it came up with some very positive and innovative proposals.
First, I want to examine the current situation in this country. Presently there are some 2.5 million Canadians who are over the age of 65. Of those, 600,000 live below the poverty line. What is critical to note is that most of those 600,000 are single and four-fifths of them, or 80 per cent, are women. They are women who, for the most part, worked full time in the home when they were younger and had little or no opportunity to prepare financially for what we so euphemistically term their "golden years". Even if they receive the full Old Age Security and guaranteed income supplement, it is a total of $534 a month or $18 a day. That amount is $2,000 below the poverty line for people living in medium-sized cities across this country, such as Kingston, Sudbury, Sydney, Kelowna and Sherbrooke. People who live in cities like those, where they receive only the Old Age Security and guaranteed income supplement payment, live $2,000 below the poverty line.
The all-Party task force on pension reform recommended that the income for single persons over the age of 65 should be set at two-thirds of the income of married couples. For those most in need, that would mean a maximum increase of $102 a month of the guaranteed income supplement. However, that increase would be based on a sliding scale downward, depending on other additional income that the pensioners might have. It meant that those most in need would receive the largest increase.
The Government chose not to accept that recommendation. Instead, the Minister of Finance in his February Budget proposed to raise the guaranteed income supplement by $25 a month on July 1 and by a further $25 a month in December. That is the proposal that the Government has brought forward and the proposal that I hope will go through Parliament. But I must ask Government Members today, where is the legislation to implement even that increase? It is less than two months before the first half of that $50 increase is supposed to take effect, yet there is no sign of any such Bill on the Order Paper. Surely the Government, with all its bureaucrats and advisers, cannot be having that much difficulty drafting such a simple piece of legislation. Surely that is not difficult. Perhaps we should ask whether it is the will to find a way that is holding the Government back.
Three years ago, the Minister of National Health and Welfare made this statement in the House of Commons, as reported at pages 8609 and 8610 of Hansard on March 25, 1981:
-we have often repeated the commitment of this Government to bring all the senior citizens who now receive the supplement over the poverty line.
Of course, she did not say when. Therein lies the deception. When statements like that are made by a Minister of the Crown, expectations are raised. The elderly poor anticipate that their burdens will be lessened, but nothing happens except that the limited income that they receive gets stretched thinner and thinner as the costs of the bare essentials of life get higher
and higher. Surely if there is any sense of decency and awareness of priorities left in the Government benches at all, it will bring in the legislation that was promised in the February Budget to increase the guaranteed income supplement.
I do not understand what the holdup is. The Government since that time has seen fit to introduce any number of other measures. Why not this one? Why has the Government not felt that this one was as necessary as any other piece of legislation that could be considered by this House? If this Opposition Day motion does nothing else but provoke the Government into taking action in this regard, we will have achieved something really worth while.

I would like to ask what are the prospects for those under the age of 65 who are still in the paid labour force or who are working full-time in the home? That subject was addressed by the all-Party task force on pension reform. The task force had two very real concerns in this regard, Mr. Speaker. One was coverage and the other was cost. It came up time and time again.
First with regard to coverage was how to reform the pension system so as to encourage and make it possible for those who are not now in retirement income plans to be able to participate in them. That was the one question we dealt with. The second was the cost of such reform, not only at the outset but the escalating cost to the public purse if these critical measures are not taken to bring all of these people who are not presently in retirement income plans into them. What would be the cost to the public purse down the road if this issue is not dealt with? We looked at the immediate costs and we looked at the long-term costs to the people of Canada. We did so, Mr. Speaker, because the problem is there before us. Old Age Security payments, public expenditure, this year amount to some $12 billion. That is a lot of money, Sir, but that amount will increase rapidly with an aging society. However, if those presently below the age of 65 are encouraged to prepare now for their retirement years, the public expenditure could be reduced.
Let me elaborate on coverage. At present, there are some 2.7 million people who work full-time in the home who have no access to the Canada Pension Plan, let alone any other pension plan. That group was of great interest to us-almost three million people who work full-time in the home. There are as well some five million people in the paid labour force who have no supplemental benefits. They pay into the Canada Pension Plan and that is it. These five million people in the paid labour force are primarily in the $10,000 to $28,000 income bracket. They work for the most part in businesses and firms which do not have pension plans, and they see RRSPs as a vehicle for higher income earners, not for themselves. Both groups that I have mentioned, those who work full-time in the home and the five million in the paid labour force who have no supplemental benefits at the present time, account for a total eight million
May 10, 1984

Canadians who are without adequate pension coverage at the moment.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has recognized the problem. She did so when she came before the parliamentary task force on March 17, 1983, and said:
I believe coverage is the key issue of pension reform. I really mean extension of coverage to all workers, and that is on a universal basis... You see, the majority of working Canadians do not belong to private pension plans. Only 54 per cent of men and 38 per cent of women in paid employment are protected by private pension plans. These are cold, hard facts.
Those were the cold, hard facts 14 months ago when the Minister said that, and they remain the same cold, hard facts today. The Minister of Finance failed to address this critical issue in his February Budget. He promised to discuss the concept of a homemaker's pension with the provinces, but he did not indicate that the federal Government was committed to bringing homemakers into the Canada Pension Plan in their own right. The Leader of my Party has made that a personal commitment.
The all-Party task force laid out in detail the way in which homemakers could be brought into the Canada Pension Plan. The Minister and his officials certainly had adequate time to study the details of the task force proposal. He must know that the recommendations stipulated that contributions for homemakers' pensions would be from family income and, where this was not possible, would be subsidized by a 0.3 per cent increase in over-all Canada Pension Plan contributions, bringing them from 3.6 per cent to 3.9 per cent of payroll. None of the cost for this would come from the public purse, but the Minister of Finance did not even react to the task force proposal in his Budget or at any time since.
Would he prefer to have the majority of those 2.7 million people who work full-time in the home being put in the position where they have to rely solely on the guaranteed income supplement when they reach the age of 65? What would that do to the public expenditure? What about the five million people in the paid labour force who have no supplemental pension plans? What encouragement was given to them to seek additional coverage? None whatsoever. Unbelievably, the changes proposed to money purchase plans by the Minister in his February Budget, which will mean a reduction in federal revenues of some $300 million annually when they come into effect, will be of greatest benefit to those earning in the upper income brackets, $55,000 or more. The changes may help those who can afford to put $10,000 per year away into such plans, but for people earning only $12,000, $15,000 or even $20,000, that idea does not particularly grab them. They simply cannot indulge in such fantasies.
Instead, the task force proposed establishing a flexible, portable, registered pension account which would have the benefit of a 40 per cent tax credit rather than a tax deduction. This incentive was aimed at encouraging lower to middle income earners, particularly women, to contribute to their own retirement income. Again, there was no response from the Minister of Finance.

In closing my remarks today, I say to the House that the parliamentary task force recognized the pressing need for real pension reform. So too did the Leader of my Party and Hon. Members on this side of the House. We realize that we cannot go on forever piling burdens of debt upon the shoulders of the next generation and the next, not if we expect the intergenerational contract to be honoured. We have to look after our elderly poor today. We have to be prepared to do more to look after ourselves tomorrow. That will only take place if those presently outside the pension system are given the opportunity and the incentive to participate. That the Government has not allowed.

Mr. Speaker, one of the great comments I hear across the country about the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government is that it is forever living for yesterday. The concern of today's elderly poor is what is of pressing need. That is what the Government should be addressing at the present time.
The Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) can go back to 1979. I can go back to the 1940s when Mr. Harris, the then Minister of Finance, became known as the "six-buck boy". It was Mr. Diefenbaker who addressed that issue. We can go back over the history of pensions from the time they began, but that is not the issue before us today. The issue today is that there are 600,000 people over the age of 65 who are living in need. The urgency is to get on with doing something about it. I say to the Hon. Member for Sudbury, who I know is concerned about this issue, that he should be pressing his Ministers to bring in this Bill and not be reminiscing about 1979, 1970, 1950 or any other year in the past. It is today that we are concerned about.

Mr. Speaker, I do not have the statistics in front of me, but I do know the concern that all of us have. I share with the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) and the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) concern for people who will be retiring and are apprehensive about their retirement income. I like the idea of a universal old age pension. Those who worked and tried to get a pension were entitled to see something across the board. There were others who tried and were not able to do it. CN pensioners received small pensions. Therefore, it made good sense to have an across-the-board pension. It helped those who were not in a position to do it to have a guaranteed income supplement. We piled one more on top of that and required people to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan.
The information I have is that the Canada Pension Plan funding is in some difficulty. There is some apprehension that in order to make it actuarially sound, we will have to increase premiums or face increased costs. Figures I have seen indicate that the time frame is not that far in the future when there will be some difficulty with the Canada Pension Plan.
I listened to the Hon. Member talk about the 0.3 per cent increase and the fact that it would not cost the Government anything. All of the items suggested by the task force involve
some cost. I am concerned that we might push something like the Canada Pension Plan costs too high by bringing in too much at once. We have the old age pension, the guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Pension Plan, which has been improved. There are more people who have access to it today. A small point is in a divorce situation, where the wife now gets half the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan, which should have been the case all along. It is there, or will be, and voluntarily some of us have to do that. The fact that I am 57 and getting closer to 65 may mean that I have a vested interest in this.
I am worried about the costs that we may be imposing on the Canada Pension Plan, all of the people who pay into it, in order to meet all the commitments that both the Hon. Member and I would eventually like to see. I am afraid that if we try to bite off more now, it may have the impact of overloading the system with costs and we will not be able to meet the benefits that should be met today.

Mr. Speaker, the concern that was expressed by the Hon. Member was expressed to the task force on many occasions. There is a perception in the public that there is something drastically wrong or inadequate about the funding of the Canada Pension Plan. Our studies did not bear that out, but they did show that the percentage of payroll that would have to be contributed to the Canada Pension Plan over the years would have to be increased. By the year 2000, we anticipated it would go up to 8 per cent of payroll. That was why we said that the proposal we put forward with regard to the inclusion of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan would be a contributory one, as with anybody else. If they contribute in the same way, they would not be asking any more or any less from the Canada Pension Plan than you or I. Nor would they contribute any less.
The question is, why should these people in Canada be treated as second-class citizens? That is what is happening at the present time with regard to the Canada Pension Plan and those who can participate in it. What we did was to make sure that this was actuarially possible. In all of the studies that we did and in everything we looked at, we were satisfied that this could be accomplished, but it would have to be on a contributory basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate in the House today. To begin with, I believe that one should first examine the point which has been raised by the Hon. Member opposite with respect to her contention that the Government has delayed the introduction of legislation to fulfil its promise to alleviate the difficulties experienced by Canada's single elderly pensioners.
I hear the word "delay" being used quite often. I think we should begin by examining the accomplishments of the Government with respect to pension reform and I think one could then conclude that it is simply not the case that there has been a delay. Contrary to what has been indicated, when examining the events of the past couple of years it becomes very clear that not only has action been taken but it has been consistent with the fulfilment of the Government's 1980 promise of pension reform.
In order to look at the history of the pension reform process, one must go back to the early part of 1981 when, shortly after the election, the National Pension Conference was convened. That conference brought together all of the players in the pension system including business, labour, government and women's groups. These players came together for the first time to look at the real problems of our pension system and to begin moving toward a national consensus on reform.
The Government followed up on the momentum established by this conference with the 1982 publication of the green paper entitled Better Pensions for Canadians. It should be noted that the proposals contained in that paper included the Government's position vis-a-vis income for the single elderly pensioner. I quote from the statement of that position:
-the situation of these single pensioners will be improved as soon as resources permit.
That same paper included a proposal to establish a parliamentary committee to undertake widespread public consultation on the issues surrounding pension reform. As the Hon. Member opposite knows, having served on that committee, that special committee on pension reform was formed on March 1, 1983. In other words, the promise to establish the committee was made in December, 1982 and fulfilled in March, 1983.
As Hon. Members know, the committee members undertook an amazing responsibility. They undertook a study of all of the
Supply
proposals contained in the Government's paper on pension reform. These not only included suggestions for changes to the public pension system of Old Age Security and Canada Pension but also included suggestions for changes to the private pension sector and changes to reflect inflation protection, the special situation of women and pensions and the financial issues associated with those proposals.
The committee heard hundreds of witnesses and scrutinized briefs from all sectors of Canadian society. All areas of vital concern to Canadians were covered thoroughly in its final report. Recommendations concerning each issue were submitted to the Government of Canada in December, 1983, and I might note that under its terms of reference the committee had an assigned reporting date of December 31, 1983. There was certainly no delay on the part of the parliamentary committee.
The Government gave its response to the parliamentary task force only two months later. This response was contained in the Budget Speech of February 15, 1984, made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). In other words, within two months the Government announced its intentions to introduce legislation to improve the financial situation of single low-income pensioners. This announcement did not contain generalized promises. It contained specific proposals to increase the guaranteed income supplement for single pensioners by $25 a month in July of 1984 and another $25 a month in December of 1984.
The same Budget also specified that the guaranteed income supplement program would be further amended to guarantee recipients of partial Old Age Security pensions the same minimum income guaranteed under the GIS program for other Canadians. I might point out to Hon. Members that the parliamentary task force had recommended further study of ways to assist these partial pensioners. The Government chose, however, not to study this issue further but instead to announce its intentions to introduce this proposal at the same time as it introduced the two-stage $50 increase in the supplement for single pensioners.
Let us examine in more detail the $50 increase in the guaranteed income supplement single rate. This increase will benefit current low-income single pensioners, widowed pensioners receiving the spouse's allowance and one-pensioner couples, about 750,000 pensioners in all. As well, some 25,000 persons whose incomes were just slightly too high to qualify for the supplement will now be entitled to receive part of the increase.
This proposed increase is by no means the first step taken to ensure income adequacy for low-income Old Age Security pensioners. In 1979, the guaranteed income supplement was increased by $20 per pensioner household. In 1980, a further increase of $35 was provided to each pensioner household. However, even though single pensioners received the full benefit of the $20 and $35 increases, for those pensioners it was not enough. Single GIS recipients, three-quarters of whom are women, were still not guaranteed an income sufficient to meet their basic needs.

May 10, 1984
Supply
Various groups and organizations, including the Royal Commission on the Status of Pensions in Ontario, the Canadian Council on Social Development and the Senate Committee on Poverty, have studied the question of benefit adequacy for singles. They all agree that a single individual needs at least 60 per cent of the income required by a couple. Given that two-pensioner couples are already guaranteed an adequate level of retirement income under the OAS-GIS program, it was decided that the guaranteed income level for single pensioners must be at least 60 per cent of the amount provided to couples. The S50 monthly increase in the guaranteed income supplement single rate will do just that. In fact, by December, 1984 this increase, along with the regular quarterly cost-of-living increases, will guarantee single low-income pensioners 62 per cent of the income guaranteed to a two-pensioner couple.
Some Hon. Members will undoubtedly question why the Government did not accept the proposal put forward by the parliamentary task force on pension reform. The task force recommended that a special top-up benefit of $102 per month, taxed back at a rate of 100 per cent, be provided only to single GIS pensioners at the lowest income levels. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, analysis showed that the Government could not accept this proposal exactly as it was put forward. The fact was that low-income Old Age Security pensioners could have been worse off than they currently are.
For instance, several provincial governments already provide top-ups to the guaranteed income supplement. These top-ups generally operate with a 50 per cent tax-back structure. This in combination with the 50 per cent tax-back rate used under the guaranteed income supplement program means that low-income pensioners already lose $1 of benefit for every $1 of other income they have. Unless the provinces agreed to fully exempt the first $102 of income a pensioner has, something which would be quite expensive to do, the pensioners with the lowest incomes would effectively lose $1.50 of benefits for every $ 1 of other income they have.
In view of this situation, it proved to be better to make a straightforward increase of $50 per month for every pensioner receiving GIS at the single rate. The wisdom of this course of action has already been proven by the announcement made by the Ontario Government that it will not only pass on this $50 to Ontario pensioners receiving the GAINS supplement but will actually add to the increase to ensure that low-income single Ontario pensioners will be guaranteed 60 per cent of the income of marrieds. That action was possible only because of the way in which the $50 increase has been designed.
I would now like to turn to the second major proposed amendment which will guarantee partial pensioners the same minimum income as provided to the full pensioner under the OAS/GIS program. Whether they have lived in Canada for 40 years or as little as 10 years, all Old Age Security pensioners will be guaranteed an adequate level of retirement income. About 3,000 persons, primarily immigrants, receiving partial OAS pensions will benefit from the proposed amendment in
the first year. This number will rise rapidly over the next ten years as more partial OAS pensioners become eligible. For example, by 1990-1991 it is estimated that as many as 25,000 persons will benefit from this amendment.
As Hon. Members know, Mr. Speaker, the Old Age Security residency rules were changed in 1977. For persons coming to Canada since that date, the old age pension is earned at the rate of one-fortieth of the full amount for each year of residency in Canada after age 18. Partial pensions were introduced to simplify the previous complex rules which not only determined entitlement on an all or nothing basis, but under which some period of residency carried more significance for eligibility purposes than others, depending on when in a person's lifetime they occurred.
The introduction of the partial benefits earned in accordance with the years of residency in Canada enables the federal Government to enter into international social security agreements. These agreements allow new Canadians to bring to Canada the pension rights they have earned in other countries. Such rights can then be combined with the rights earned here to meet eligibility rules for Canadian benefits, such as the ten-year requirement for an OAS. Right now we have agreements in force with five countries; Italy, France, Portugal, Greece and Jamaica. We anticipate an agreement with the United States will become effective this year. In fact, Mr. Speaker, just at this moment the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is in Belgium to sign a similar agreement with that country.
As well, we have negotiations under way with a number of other countries. However, despite progress in this regard, it remains that some pensioners do not have access to foreign pension income, nor income from any other source. As a result, they have nothing to fill the gap between the partial old age pension they receive and the amount of the full pension which lifelong Canadian residents receive.
Significantly, Old Age Security pensioners receiving a partial benefit can receive maximum GIS benefits. However, because they do not receive full basic pensions, partial pensioners are guaranteed less total income than is guaranteed to persons who have lived in Canada all of their lives. The proposed amendment will mean that low-income pensioners receiving partial OAS benefits will qualify for whatever additional guaranteed income supplement benefits are necessary to give them the same minimum income level as other pensioners. This change will eliminate any adverse consequences which could have arisen as a result of the amendments to the OAS Act in 1977. As well, it is consistent with the goals of the guaranteed income supplement program, namely, ensuring income adequacy to all pensioners in Canada.
There is no doubt that every Hon. Member of this House would have been happy to see this legislation introduced earlier. The needs of the low-income elderly have been known to all of us. However, the economic circumstances of a worldwide recession made it necessary for the Government to wait until it could responsibly make the commitment implied by the $50 increase in the GIS single rate. This increase is going to
May 10, 1984

take place beginning this July. That is an undertaking which was given in the February Budget and is one which was not given lightly.
Hon. Members know that thousands of pensioners are now counting on this increase. They also know that the Government will bring the legislation forward shortly, Why, then, is there now this suggestion of delay? What can be accomplished, Mr. Speaker, by this suggestion except to create needless anxiety among our pensioners? Pensioners, Mr. Speaker, have enough to contend with in making ends meet without worrying that somehow the promised increase will be denied to them. I know that Hon. Members from the benches opposite will want to reassure pensioners that when this legislation is brought forward, it will be given speedy consideration.
For our part, Mr. Speaker, I can assure Hon. Members of this House, and all Canadians, that the Government of Canada remains committed to these promises and that the introduction of the proposed legislation is imminent. With the co-operation of all Hon. Members, the legislation can be passed quickly, and since Opposition Members have expressed their support for these proposals, I have no hesitation in assuring low-income single pensioners that they will see the S25 increase in their GIS pension cheques in July.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) for moving a motion allowing the House to look at the Liberal record on pension issues and the most recent inappropriate response to the serious poverty experience of many elderly women, and the totally inadequate response to the demonstrated need for pension reform.
One in four elderly Canadians live in poverty. Some 60 per cent of single elderly women, 80 per cent of them widows, are poor with little opportunity, other than through increases to the OAS or GIS, to see any improvement in their standard of living. They look forward to a long life of poverty, as do many women working today inside and outside the home, unless real pension reform is implemented. The NDP concurs with the motion regretting the delay in recognizing the needs of hundreds of thousands of single elderly poor by failing to implement increases to the GIS or increasing the universal OAS to its former level of importance in income replacement.
However, just like the Conservatives, we also recognize that electoral considerations mean more to the governing Liberal Party than the needs of pensioners. It did not require a
parliamentary task force on pension reform to show the Government the serious shortcomings of our public and private system in providing adequate pensions for women who statistically outlive their husbands and who have little opportunity to contribute to their own private plans or earn enough to achieve full CPP or even to share a working spouse's pension on divorce or death. When the Government does respond on the eve of an election, the response denies the seriousness of the conditions many Canadians find themselves in. By rejecting the task force report recommendation of a $102 permanent increase in the GIS for the single elderly, and only promising a $50 per month increase by year end, the Government fails to understand the report itself and the witnesses who appeared before the task force. Failure to introduce the changes to the House compounds the uncertainty many Canadians feel.
While the NDP can also sympathize with the second part of the motion condemning the Government on its response to the task force report on pension reform, we cannot share the Hon. Member's surprise at the pension reform offered by the February, 1984 Budget. The response of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is consistent with the philosophy of the majority report of the Liberals and the Conservatives providing more incentives and another chance for the private sector to respond to a shameful record. Increases in tax incentives to wealthy Canadians to encourage greater participation should not surprise the Hon. Member, nor should the feeble response to a greater pension coverage for low-income and part-time workers through a registered pension account. The Member and her Conservative colleagues join the majority of Liberal Members in seeking any and all methods to protect private pensions from meaningful expansion of the Canada Pension Plan or Old Age Security. Instead of meaningful reform, the Liberals have responded with a token GIS increase amounting to $1.61 per day by the end of 1984, while providing massive tax deductions to high-income earners which could amount in the most extreme cases to an equivalent of $20 per day to wealthy individuals.
Unlike the Liberals or Conservatives, the NDP would implement a pension system to reduce the dependence on the GIS, as was the original intent when the GIS was established on a temporary basis in 1966 while the Government waited for the Canada Pension Plan, Quebec Pension Plan and private plans to mature in order to reduce dependency on the GIS. Some 18 years later, in 1984, over 50 per cent of retired Canadians depend on full or partial guaranteed income supplement. This is evidence of the failure of the private and public sector pension systems in the past two decades.
Pension reform should indeed be reform. The proposals in the Budget insist on another decade or two of dependence on private plans to meet the needs of Canadians. It will not happen. We need to reaffirm the universality of the Old Age Security pension and return it towards its 1964 level of income replacement of 20 per cent of the average industrial wage, thereby beginning to reduce the dependence on GIS and the disincentives to saving for retirement which the 50 per cent tax-back on additional income attached to the GIS causes.
May 10, 1984

Liberal leadership candidates and Conservative leaders and former leadership candidates leave many doubts about their intentions towards universal pension arrangements. People wonder how deficits are going to be slashed while politicians advocate billions of dollars of additional expenditures to appease every special interest group on the economic side. The social development envelope of the Cabinet accounts for 40 per cent of the federal expenditures with another 20 per cent used to pay off the debt incurred by successive Liberal Governments.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, in whose name the motion stands today, made an appropriate statement to the House yesterday with regard to the comments of leadership candidate Mr. John Turner about slashing the deficit by $15 billion over the next three to seven years. She said:
The candidate refuses to spell out in detail how he would accomplish his goal, but mere mention of his intention to go after social programs has already had a damaging effect. For while economists may be skeptical about his statement, hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have to get by on the guaranteed income supplement and social assistance, are now worried that their payments will be radically reduced.
I think that is a valid comment, Mr. Speaker. The Member for Kingston and the Islands is also aware, as is the public, that many members of her own Party feel social expenditures are too high. They are itching to get into power to switch Government priorities to the corporate sector. Her Party worries the very people she is concerned about in her statement. It is possible that a John Turner-led Liberal Party would be undistinguishable from a Brian Mulroney-led Conservative Party.
In fact, some of the comments of the former Finance Minister give a lot of people concern and doubt about what the policies really are. On November 25, 1983 Mr. Crosbie said, "We're not giving anything away. If you want to find out what our policies are, elect us". On July 12, 1983 the same individual is quoted in Maclean's as saying: "If I told you what I would do we would never get elected". Mr. Speaker, those comments do not engender any confidence in people who are living on public pensions or even private pensions.
The NDP issued a dissenting view in the parliamentary task force report on pension reform outlining both areas of support for the majority view, but disagreeing fundamentally on the majority faith in giving private plans yet another chance to apply their pensions to the two-thirds of women not presently covered, to offer inflation protection, to provide mobility to workers moving into new jobs, and to securing employer contributions to workers' pensions before 10 years of service.
We called for a 25 per cent increase in the Old Age Security pension to 17.5 per cent of the average industrial wage, indexed to wages to protect its universality and its earlier significance in replacing pre-retirement earnings. We also called for an expansion of the Canada Pension Plan to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage. The recommendation to expand the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan
Supply
conformed to the request of women's groups, labour groups, social policy groups and some pensioner organizations fed up with the promises of private pensions and aware of the experiences under reliance on those same private pensions.
In its presentation the National Action Committee on the Status of Women told the task force:
For the future elderly women, the most important reform would be the expansion of the Canada Pension Plan, so that those who are in the labour force can have adequate benefits when they get to the age of 65.
Many other women's groups advocated increases in the Canada Pension Plan to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage.
In rejecting any expansion of the Canada Pension Plan, Liberal and Conservative Members ignored the experience of labour, women and pensioners toward a system that has failed to respond voluntarily to the demands of Canadians. Instead, we now have proposals in a Budget document which threaten further government action if voluntary compliance with increased participation in private plans is not evident over some uncertain period of time. Failure to take on the powerful pension lobby will mean continuing dependence on government assistance through GIS and tax assistance.
The only carrot for women, those most in need of pension reform, is the promise to discuss the principle of homemakers' pensions with provincial governments. Even the promise of a homemaker pension advocated by some, but by no means all, women's groups is flawed. It is flawed not only because it favours one-earner couples, but is flawed in the majority report because it fails to recommend increasing the CPP/QPP beyond the present 25 per cent of the average industrial wage. The Government has accepted this recommendation and denied the most important reforms for women in the pension field. This particularly affects women in part-time work or women in jobs with no private pension plans. At this time only one-third of women are in private plans despite the growing number of women attached to the work force.
I would like to spend some time discussing part-time workers because once again the Budget proposals calling for pension reform offer nothing to the vast majority of the 2.7 million part-time workers in Canada, 72 per cent of whom are women. The inclusion of part-time workers in pension plans, where offered to full-time employees, and the provision of a locked-in registered pension account will not significantly benefit the one in five Canadians expected to comprise the parttime work force in Canada by the end of the century. These workers earning less than 80 per cent of full-time worker wages are not likely to respond to the lucrative tax deductions of the new and improved RRSPs, or to be very interested in locking in pension funds to a registered pension account.
In publishing their report on part-time work, the Commission of Inquiry on Part-time Work recommended the following:
In view of the lack of Pension coverage in industries where most part-time workers are found, the above recommendations cannot be guaranteed to provide all part-time workers with adequate retirement income. Therefore, the federal Government should work towards expanding the public earnings-related pension

May 10, 1984
Supply
system (CPP/QPP) to replace a higher percentage of pre-retirement earnings, preferably, 40 to 50 per cent of the Average Industrial Wage. At the same time, a method should be found to offset to higher contribution rates for low income workers, many of whom are part-time workers.
The recommendation referred to in that quote applies to changes in the Labour Code requiring part-time workers to be included in fringe benefits and pension plans on a pro-rated basis. The problem, of course, is that few employees in the community, business and personal services sector are pension plan members.
Workers in the home or outside the home will not be well served by Liberal promises of pension reform, or for that matter by Conservative Party proposals dependent upon the accumulation of 25 to 30 years of pension contributions before any reasonable amount of inflation protection can be expected.
By rejecting retroactive inflation protection, the 60 per cent CPI inflation protection recommended in the Budget will only apply on contributions made after the implementation of reform discussion, both federally and provincially. Pensioners will continue to see serious erosion of their retirement income earned from private plans for the next 30 to 40 years while once again we wait for private plans to mature, this time through registered pension accounts, inflation protection and earlier vesting.
Instead of improving pensions by increasing contributions and benefits to the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans which provide immediate inflation protection, complete mobility, immediate vesting and application to part-time as well as full-time workers, the Government is willing to risk more years of inadequate post-retirement income for pensioners.
I would like to deal now with the financing of the Quebec and Canada Pension Plans because the detractors of public pensions, such as the National Citizens' Coalition and many Liberal and Conservative Members of Parliament, would have Canadians believe the plan is bankrupt.
Canadians contribute 3.6 per cent of their incomes up to the average industrial wage into the CPP/QPP to provide themselves with a pension of 25 per cent up to the maximum of the AIW which is currently $20,000. These contributions, which are then loaned to provincial governments, have accumulated over $23 billion as of 1983. This accumulation of assets is based on a relatively low contribution rate, one of which was anticipated to increase as early as 1976 but has not done so because current contributions to the plan are adequate to pay benefits to retired plan members. Provinces in fact, up until this time, have not been required to pay interest on the loans from CPP/QPP although they may soon have to. Currrent contributions are adequate for the next 20 years without the fund being bankrupted, as some people would have us believe.
The conclusion of the parliamentary task force was to reject the suggestion that the Canada Pension Plan was bankrupt or suspect because the assets securing its promises are not carried on the books of private corporations. The task force recognized that the capacity of the Canadian economy to meet pension
commitments decades from now depends more on our ability to move grain along rail lines, goods through seaways and data via satellites, than does it depend on paper gains that make pension fund managers look good in the short run.
If there are fears about the willingness of provinces to pay back the accumulated loans from the Canada Pension Plan, these fears should be directed at the provinces and not at the Canada Pension Plan, which is functioning as originally intended through a transfer of pension benefits from one generation to the other on a basically pay-as-you-go basis, with no intention to accumulate massive funds through full funding of the plan. In fact, the business sector is adamantly opposed to full funding of the CPP for fear of impact on their own capital markets and government control of huge amounts of pension funds. The CPP/QPP funding mechanism is in fact designed to satisfy the business community and the federal and provincial governments.
Canada's pension system should be expected to meet certain objectives. I believe most expect that we should be able to ensure that Canadians are able to avoid serious disruptions in their standard of living upon retirement or upon the death of a retired spouse. Elderly Canadians should also be provided with a reasonable guaranteed minimum income and with pension opportunities and arrangements that are fair.
By expanding the Canada Pension Plan to meet a greater replacement rate, these criteria can be met without the delay and inadequacies inherent in private sector reform alone. When combined with an Old Age Security increase, Canada Pension Plan expansion and credit splitting, homemakers and part-time workers will be guaranteed better pensions. At page 150 of the minority report I have outlined certain things that will accrue to single elderly people and women in general if in fact the NDP recommendations for increasing Old Age Security and the Canada Pension Plan do in fact accrue. Full-time homemakers will be guaranteed an indexed income above the poverty line. If their spouse was a middle or low-income earner, they will be guaranteed that their standard of living will be maintained when their spouse moves from work to retirement.
Third, homemakers will be guaranteed that their standard of living will be maintained when their spouse dies. They will be provided with the Canada Pension Plan retirement benefits in their own names at age 65. Finally, they will be guaranteed equal treatment with their spouses no matter which one dies first.
We are also anxious to see legislation brought before the House which will at least deal with the most critical problem that elderly Canadians face right now. They are the 600,000 people who live below the poverty line, four-fifths of whom are women, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. We are skeptical about the time frame for introducing this Bill before Parliament. We certainly have much to say about pension reform and we will be doing so when changes are brought before Parliament.
Specifically, we will be very concerned and will want to know in detail why the Government can find massive amounts
May 10, 1984

of money to increase the tax deductions for high-income earners when it can only find $50 per month for single elderly pensioners and cannot even pass that measure without great delay in the House of Commons.
Once again I thank the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands for providing the House of Commons with what I believe is probably the most important issue facing Canadians today, not only elderly Canadians living in poverty but the entire population which must decide on reforming a pension system that has been woefully inadequate over the last 20 years.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for that question because I think it is important. Members on the task force had certain concerns themselves about the Canada Pension Plan, its mechanism for funding and its loans to provincial governments. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. You have not aborted my take-off; I am quite prepared to take off at this time.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) because it is a pertinent topic. I would like to illustrate to the House and the people of Canada how the Liberal Party's use of the words "pension reform" is really a question of mirrors, illusion and smokescreens. The Government has absolutely no intention of bringing in pension reform.
Let us review the history of what the Liberal Government has done in this regard. It is a very brief history. Shortly after it was elected in February of 1980, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), with much fanfare through newspaper advertisements and so on, said that the Government would hold a National Pension Conference. This conference took place a year later, in the spring of 1981. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the then Minister of Finance as well as the Minister of National Health and Welfare appeared at that conference and assured all of the delegates that pension reform was a subject that the Liberal Party would urgently address.
In fact, the Liberal Party made two promises. First, it promised that there would be a conference of first ministers held immediately in order to discuss pension reform. That was in 1981, yet when did that first ministers' conference take place? We are still waiting for it. So much for that particular promise. Second, it promised that it would publish a green paper on pensions within three months. We waited for the entire year of 1981 and much of 1982. I believe we received the green paper toward the end of 1982. This report is contained in a nice glossy booklet. All that we see from the Liberals about pension reform are glossy booklets in both official languages. There is nothing essentially wrong with what is in the book. It was just a repeat of what occurred at the National Pension Conference. There are some things that are wrong, however, but what it did in all of its glossy paper, small books and big books, was to set out what those of us who are involved in pensions already know, that reform was needed.
In the index we find the following comments. Elderly Canadians should be guaranteed a reasonable minimum income; everyone can agree with that. Here is another phrase: "Opportunities and arrangements available to Canadians should be fair to provide for their income". Canadians should be able to avoid serious disruption of their pre-retirement living standards on retirement.
Here is the booklet, Mr. Speaker, and here is the information. This is a very political Party that we have across the way. Its members were not sure who supported this proposal and who supported that proposal. There is at the end of this book a proposal about which they were concerned. The Minister of

May 10, 1984
Supply
National Health and Welfare said: "There is a large question of coverage and I think it should be handled one of two ways. One is to increase the CPP and the other is to make mandatory private pensions". That was the real issue behind the green paper and it was the real issue behind the proposal to set up the parliamentary task force. I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not expect the task force to come up with anything new, but she did expect it to come up with an endorsement of one of those two proposals.
The task force was set up. It reported within a year after a lot of hard work. What happened? It came up with another glossy piece of paper, this time light blue in colour. The social reporters commented that it was a Conservative report. I do not know whether they were talking about the content of the report or the blue label. In any event, the report was well received. The task force did a lot of good work. It set up a very comprehensive scheme for Canadians but it did not do what the Minister of National Health and Welfare wanted it to do. The task force did not endorse mandatory pensions in the private sector, nor did it endorse an increase to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage in the Canada Pension Plan. I can get into that later but I can tell you very good reasons why it did not do that, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister received the report. Her comment was that it did not speak to coverage. But it did speak to coverage in a very efficient way. As so well pointed out by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), it had some very imaginative proposals for dealing with low-income people.
We waited. Then we had the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). We have some more glossy paper. This time it is brown glossy paper. The books have all sorts of nice brown colours on them. There is a very happy couple in the springtime of their retirement shown on the front cover of one. The document again goes all through the lip service and illusions and everything else about which we have heard so much, but the document does not get to the meat of the problem. The proposals do not provide a decent minimum coverage for elderly people. They do not come near that. The proposal of $50 a month over a year still leaves, as the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands said, 600,000 elderly people about $2,000 under the poverty line.
This Government has created illusions and given us smokescreens. It is not really serious. I could ask the question that Mondale asked Senator Hart: "Where is the beef in your program?" Where is the legislation? Surely the Government can bring it forward, Mr. Speaker. We have heard silly excuses from the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell), whom I respect and who was ill at ease when he gave the kind of excuses such as: "The Opposition is not finishing the work with the other legislation and we cannot bring this essential legislation forward". I cannot buy that explanation at all.
Let me come back to why the task force did not follow the Minister's hope and provide an increase in the Canada Pension Plan to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage that was in the minority report. The simple reason, which should be clear
to all Canadians, is that at the moment the Canada Pension Plan costs the average person 3.6 per cent of his income; 1.8 per cent is usually paid by the individual employee and 1.8 per cent is usually paid by the employer. A self-employed person pays the whole premium. But that is not a true cost. If the Canada Pension Plan were properly funded, it would cost the average worker 10 per cent of his or her income. Someone may ask from where is that money coming. At the moment we are transferring it to future generations. We are not really covering, with the 3.6 per cent contribution to the CPP, the real cost. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is the best bargain anybody ever had in this country.
The New Democratic Party's proposal, which was really the proposal of the Canadian Labour Congress written by a Canadian Labour Congress official, is for an increase to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage. That works out to 20 per cent of a true funded cost. We in the task force were not prepared to have a young taxpayer with a mortgage on his house and raising a family pay 20 per cent of his income, to be transferred to the same generation. There was a consensus throughout the land. The only people who wanted it were those who did not concern themselves about the cost. I remember bringing this point forward in Calgary to a union group. The answer given was: "I am not worried about the cost; where the money comes from is your problem". That is the kind of attitude which the task force could not quite buy.
What about the other proposal which the Minister would have us accept for coverage, namely mandate to the private sector regarding the necessity of providing pensions. In Canada the majority of small businesses do not have pension plans. It is also a fact that the small business community at this time is going through a very difficult period. Small business in Canada provides 80 per cent of the new jobs. I think that figure is fairly accurate. The task force was not prepared to impose additional costs on that segment of the business sector because we felt small businesses were having enough difficulty with the taxes and the paperwork for Stat-sCanada and so on. It was not the time, if it ever is. Small business should be given an opportunity through the proposals put forth in the task force report to provide those pensions.
Certainly the majority of the members felt that the philosophy behind pensions was that people should be encouraged to provide their own. It should be made easy for them to do so. One should not impose stringent regulations and high costs on one generation to be passed to another.
That is why the task force did not do what the Minister hoped. It is my understanding that there are presently discussions taking place between the federal Government and the provinces. It is also my understanding that when they reach an agreement they will propose some changes in the Canada Pension Plan, perhaps somewhat like those proposed by the task force which were taken up in the Budget papers of the last Budget. But I want to warn Members of this House and Canadians that if that happens they can expect an increase in the cost of their monthly payments, an increase of that 3.6 per cent contribution.
May 10, 1984

I contend-some people do not agree with me-that the Canada Pension Plan in its present form is really a fraud on Canadians. It is not a pension plan at all. It is merely a system of taxation to get money into the general revenue fund of each province and then there is an obligation by the Government to say: "Fine, we will pay out these funds".
The Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) tried to say that the Canada Pension Plan is not in trouble and that payments should be increased. But what are the facts, Mr. Speaker? Most people in Canada think there is a fund available somewhere as a result of the 3.6 per cent they pay toward the CPP. However, they are very shocked and surprised to learn there is no fund and that any moneys which have proportionately gone to the provinces have been used by the provinces in their general revenue funds. What have they done with that money? They have built roads, they have hired bureaucrats, perhaps they have built schools, and they have lent money to their Crown corporations. Only one province has kept an accurate accounting of where the money has gone. Only one province has made plans to pay it back. Other provinces have said that they are quite capable of paying back the money any time they want, but others have said that they will not pay it back. Of course, some provinces have said that they need that money coming in or they would be not able to survive, so they are the ones who are very interested in seeing it continue.
We do not have a fully-funded plan. The reason for this is that if we had such a plan, it would cost 10 per cent instead of 3.6 per cent. By now $75 billion would have been built up in the fund and it would be in the hands of government. Indeed that would be very dangerous. Who wants government spending $75 billion? They would control all private companies in Canada with that amount of money.
That is the type of situation which exists in Sweden where almost 50 per cent of new capital belongs to the government because of pension funds. Political parties vie to obtain control of that fund. This is why I think no reasonable person would want a fully-funded pension plan.
The task force recommended a pay-as-you-go plan with a cushion of two or three years. That is not what we have in Canada, as the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni said. We have a partially-funded plan. In fact, it is overfunded to the extent of $25 billion right now. I suggest it would be very difficult to get that money back. It is almost impossible for any provincial government to start raising that amount of money and paying it back. They simply will not do it because it is much easier to say that they will improve benefits and increase contribution rates. I guarantee that is what will happen very quickly; we will probably see that in June. The rate they propose will probably be more than that of a pay-as-you-go plan.
At the moment the plan is taking in as much as it is paying out. As I understand it, if the contribution rate is not increased, next year we will be asking the provinces to pay
Supply
their interest into the plan. So far they have paid interest into the plan and have borrowed it back out again, without it ever reaching the people who should receive the benefits. If the provinces pay back the interest, the plan would not need to be subsidized nor would the contributions need to be increased until about 1991, at which stage they would have to start paying back the $25 billion to keep the plan solvent. I believe that would be gone by the year 2001. In point of fact, if we said that there were to be no further contributions and that the provinces had to pay back the interest and what they owed, the plan would continue without any increase until the year 2001.
The task force did not feel that was a good idea because it would involve a large increase. It felt that the increase in contributions should be gradual, and that is why the major recommendation was that the plan should be phased in over a 25-year period. It was felt that the Government and the provinces should set the rate over the 25 years and review it every five years to ensure that their calculations are correct and that people do not face a sudden increase. Unfortunately, that particular plan will not be accepted because of the difficulties in which the provinces find themselves.
There are those who argue that the provinces should have the money just as much as the private sector, that social capital is just as effective at creating wealth as private capital. That may well be true. I do not think I am prepared to argue that, but the fact of the matter is that a lot of that money was not used as social capital in the sense of building roads, schools, hospitals and dams. Much of it went into the hiring of bureaucrats. Perhaps, with access to easily available money, governments spent more than they would have normally and became involved in spending patterns which we are now trying to avoid.
In negotiations with the provinces, Parliament and the Government have to be very careful. If the Government were so impressed with pension reform, it would have indicated what kind of stance it was taking in its negotiations with the provinces. When this plan was first started-and I will give it credit-the federal Government wanted contributions to be around 1 per cent or 1.5 per cent. It felt that that percentage would be sufficient to fund the plan on a pay-as-you-go basis. However, it gave in to the provinces in order to get its hands on pensions, which are a provincial responsibility. Of course the provinces, God bless them, took as much as they could. This is why the rate was set at 3.6 per cent. They had good statisticians. They knew there would be a large build-up in the fund and that they would have money to spend.
This is why I say that it is a fraud on taxpayers. It is a regressive tax. Those things that they would normally build with social capital, such as schools and churches-perhaps they do not build churches; perhaps in Newfoundland they build churches-are paid for by people with $20,000 incomes. A person with a $20,000 income pays 3.6 per cent of his income to provide such things, whereas a person with a $40,000 income pays 1.8 per cent. Is that fair or reasonable? Yet the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni says that he wants this figure increased to 50 per cent of the average

May 10, 1984
Supply
income. That is even more regressive. It is just ridiculous. If we want to go that route, it would be much better to call it a tax and make everyone pay it. It could be a 3.6 per cent or 4 per cent tax against everyone's income, but that is too honest. Governments do not like to be honest. It is too direct. People might understand what is being done to them and would become very unhappy.
I see my time is almost up. Like the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni, I commend the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I think this Parliament and the people of Canada know that if this Government brings in any pension reforms, particularly with respect to women, it will have been due to the efforts of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. I hope she continues the fight.

speechtext: Questions or comments?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to hear the comments of my friend from the task force. However, in rejecting any increase in the Canada Pension Plan and any mandating in the private sector, the Hon. Member did not refer to the additional 50 per cent of the people who at the present time are not covered by private pension plans. In terms of the suggestions either in the Government's budget proposals or in the task force report, how can the Hon. Member see more reliance on the private sector as more opportunity for people to save for retirement if there is no increase in the public pension system or some mandating in the private system?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to that question, I really do not see anything in the Budget proposals of the Government to solve that problem. There was a considerable number of proposals in the report of the task force. One was RPAs and another was to provide tax credits for people investing in RRSPs. In other words, it would attract the lower income group and make it worth while for them to be involved in a self-help program. In fact, most small businesses today want to become involved in pension schemes, but they want them to be flexible. They do not want them to be mandated. They want people to go into them as they can afford to do so.
You will find, Mr. Speaker, that the response to the registered pension account is very large. In fact, I give the green paper credit for that proposal. The Government brought that proposal forward as an afterthought. It was not very serious, but it was grabbed. Everywhere you went, people were enthusiastic about this. It was made a much more important part of the process than one would have thought. That is why the task force felt there was a real potential here. That is where the coverage for those people will exist. The task force proposal for married people would bring a large number of people into the pension scheme.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the problems is the locked-in aspect of a registered pension account. Once that contribution has been made by the employer and the employee, that is
locked in until retirement. That will be a massive disincentive to people on the low-income scale.
The RRSP is already available to individuals and could have been used by employers to give a pension over the last few years. Why does the Hon. Member feel there will be any greater take-up of an RPA than there has been initiatives by private employers to initiate RRSPs for their employees?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is why the Government proposal in the Budget will not work. I agree there is some incentive because it is a locked-in program. That is why the task force suggested the RRSP be frozen and only RPAs be allowed in the future.
Let us examine what we are doing here. We are giving tax credits to people who save for retirement. Once a pension, always a pension. There have been too many examples in the past of people using their RRSPs when they take a leave of absence for a year. They spend the money without having to pay the high taxes. The state may have to support them anyway. If we give them tax breaks for pension accounts, it should be kept in a pension. That is basic.
That is why I am so upset about the Government proposal to increase pensions for those receiving over $50,000. It is the tax dollars of someone earning $20,000 that will pay for the privilege these people will get. That is ridiculous. I might say while I have the opportunity that it is a bureaucrat's proposal. The only reason it is there is because most bureaucrats earn more than $50,000 a year and they want bigger and fatter pensions. That is obviously why they did it.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the very informative and excellent address of the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer). I cannot help but remember the days when he was Mayor of the City of Edmonton and I was one of his constituents. He showed great concern for the rank and file, and he still has that concern. That is why I will ask this question.
There is quite a body of people who will never qualify for a pension because they are not able to contribute, such as housewives and women who stay home to look after a crippled brother, an aged father or a sick mother. They have paid nothing into the Canada Pension Plan.
Several years ago there was a federal disability pension and a provincial one. One almost had to be cold before he got the federal pension. The provincial pension filled in the gap for those who could not work. Today there are people who reach the age where they cannot work, they have no pension and do not know what to do. All they get is welfare.
Did the task force give consideration to this group of people who have never had the opportunity to pay into the Canada Pension Plan and consequently cannot expect to get anything out of it? Will this group always be left high and dry, or do we have something in mind to help them in the years when they need help?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his kind words. The task force did in fact deal with this. As the
May 10, 1984

Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands suggested, the proposal to put married people, men and women, into the pension scheme would include a large portion of those people. We made several proposals to push back the age of eligibility for spouse's allowance, dependant's allowance and survivor's allowance to age 60 in order to fill that gap. We made proposals on disability pensions. We made many proposals which this Government has not taken up.
There is no doubt that the area the Hon. Member mentions is a very serious one. To a large degree it may not be a pension problem but a social welfare problem. Whatever name you call it, a reasonable government has a responsibility to look after these people. We cannot spend all kinds of time and money on corporations and on looking after executives of air companies and then ignore these people.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: PLEA FOR RELEASE OF MART NIKLUS BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in February of this year we were informed of the desperate situation of Estonian dissident Mart Niklus, who had been imprisoned by Soviet authorities for his human rights activities. My plea today is probably a last effort to obtain this man's release. Already in poor health from his previous prison terms for human rights activities, he was again imprisoned in 1981 for another 10 years of hard labour and five years of internal exile. After engaging in a hunger strike in October of last year, he has now begun another hunger strike.
I ask the House can a free nation such as Canada stand by helplessly while the Soviet Union persecutes with impunity those who stand up for their rights, rights which we often seem to take for granted, and rights for which people living under Soviet oppression are willing to die? Mart Niklus has already been granted an entrance visa into Canada. On behalf of all
Canadians of Estonian heritage, and indeed on behalf of all people of the free world who believe in the freedoms of the individual, I urge the House to do all in its power to obtain Mart Niklus' release and allow him to emigrate to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada has recently released, in 10 different languages its demographic profile of Ontario entitled "Ontario Highlights from the 1981 Census". The 1981 census contains a huge array of information on the social, cultural, and economic characteristics of Canadians. The majority of highlights in the demographic profile of Ontario were compiled from the longer form which one-fifth of Canadian householders were asked to complete. The census gives Canadians an in-depth and accurate profile of themselves, as well as detailing how political representation is to be distributed in the House of Commons.
"Ontario Highlights from the 1981 Census" has been printed in the following 10 languages: English, French, German, Ukrainian, Polish, Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and Greek. I feel that Statistics Canada should be commended for making its census data available in so many different languages. An achievement such as this underscores the federal Government's commitment to continuing a practical and progressive implementation of multiculturalism into the fabric of daily Canadian life.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, every time I raise the topic of multiculturalism I get nothing but hoots, howls, and derision from members of the Progressive Conservative Party. In the next election the people of Canada will show their disrespect for that kind of attitude toward a policy of multiculturalism.

subtopic: CALL FOR MEASURES TO ENSURE INDUSTRY'S SURVIVAL
CALL FOR MEASURES TO ENSURE INDUSTRY'S SURVIVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian of Ukrainian descent I am very pleased to speak on behalf of my Party on a very important national topic. As this is National Forest Week, it is a good time for Canadians to face up to the reality that we are destroying our forests and the jobs that go with the vital forestry industry.
The Canadian Forestry Service was once a proud world leader in forestry research and management techniques. This golden age of the federal Forestry Service was encouraged and supported by the Diefenbaker Government in 1960. Since the advent of the Liberal Government in the mid-1960s, there has been an inverse relationship between the length of time the

May 10, 1984
Liberals have been in power and the amount of real support that has been given to the forestry sector. In most respects the treatment of our forests over the past two decades has been an ignoble sham.
Increased public awareness, and solid representation and support from members of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, have brought forestry issues to the fore. The Government must respond to these issues. It must take significant steps to secure the survival of a $24 billion Canadian industry that supports one million Canadian jobs.
The Government of Canada must take the lead. It must commit itself to acting to restore forestry to departmental rank, and to working co-operatively with the provinces, territories and industries to secure this vital component of Canada's future. Without this commitment, National Forest Week will become a week of national mourning.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning we were honoured to receive the Hon. Minister before the Standing Committee on Transport. The Minister came to table his new policy, Canada's policy on air transportation. Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all my constituents in the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe area, I must say I am delighted with the proposals that were made and that are being submitted to the Canadian people.
Basically, this policy demonstrates the Government's confidence in the ability of Canada's air transportation industry to sustain increased competition. With the Minister, I would say that the airlines will now have an opportunity to be more productive and more competitive. Consumers will thus benefit from a wider range of prices and services.
I would also like to draw the attention of my fellow Canadians to the fact that deregulation of air fares and air routes does not apply to safety regulations, which must be observed at all times in air transportation.
