subtopic: DEMAND FOR INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
DEMAND FOR INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for several months the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board have been promising prairie farmers the return of some of their contributions to the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. Both opposition Parties have indicated that there is agreement to assist in making speedy changes to the Act to make it more responsive to the income needs of farmers.
More than two weeks ago the two Ministers issued a nine-page press release outlining the effect of their proposed legislation on farmers. They indicated how the per unit trigger mechanism would be more sensitive to price declines, how a full change to a crop year basis would more accurately reflect costs and speed up pay-outs, and how the five-year crop averaging period would yield larger pay-outs of up to $300 million. For a farmer who has contributed the maximum levy, that would amount to a pay-out of about $5,000.
That is what the Ministers have said, Mr. Speaker, but they have done nothing since. There has been no Bill placed before the House, and no concrete action has been taken to show that the Ministers really mean to make a pay-out now when farmers need it.
Why has the Bill not been presented to the House? Why must farmers wait to get their own money back? Why does the Minister continue to delay the pay-out? Does he intend for the pay-out to be seen only as an election campaign goody rather than as an entitlement for which pre-payment was made by western farmers in good faith?

subtopic: CALL FOR RESTORATION OF FREEDOM OF CHOICE
CALL FOR RESTORATION OF FREEDOM OF CHOICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, western Canada was surveyed in square miles, our roads are built and measured in miles, our farms are measured in acres and sections, and our agricultural products are bought and sold in gallons and pounds and tons. Where it was necessary, for example, in the sale of wheat to metric countries, for years the conversion was made at the time of sale by the Wheat Board. Everyone was happy, that is, except for this totalitarian oriented Liberal Government which brought in compulsory metric. The provincial Governments were duped into accepting it, and farmers then received their wheat cheques based on tonnes and, in spite of the utter confusion that resulted, acres were replaced with fractional hectares, and miles with kilometres.
"I am a stranger in my own country", a farmer said to me. "The Government suddenly changed the measurements that I learned in school and used all my life. Now I don't know what I'm selling or what I am getting for a bushel".
Well one provincial Government has now come to its senses and at least has made a start in reflecting the thinking of its people. This year the Alberta Government ordered that all publications and material printed by government Departments be in acres as well as hectares when referring to land measurements.
Sir John A. Macdonald in 1871 gave Canadians freedom of choice to use imperial or metric. Will this Liberal Government now disband the Metric Commission which has provided loyal Liberals with high paying jobs, costing Canadians more than $50 million, and restore the freedom of choice provided by Sir John?

May 10, 1984
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I direct my question to the Minister of State for Finance. Would the Minister of State indicate if he feels it is inconsistent government policy, on the one hand to attempt to create employment and, on the other hand, follow a high interest pattern, bearing in mind that for every 1 per cent increase in our prime rate 25,000 Canadian jobs are ended? It is like putting out of work all of those working for British Columbia Packers Limited, the Campbell Soup Company Ltd., Canadian Tire Corp., Coca-Cola Ltd., Dome Petroleum, McCain Foods Limited, and McDonnell Douglas Canada Ltd., all in one fell swoop. How can the Minister justify that kind of interest rate structure?

Mr. Speaker, no one rejoices at higher interest rates. We do not on this side of the House. I am sure that the Hon. Member does not either. No one can be happy with increases in interest rates, but the Hon. Member opposite should understand that interest rates in Canada are a direct reflection of interest rates in the United States.
The Hon. Member knows full well that in the United States interest rates over the past months have been increasing as a result of two factors; high government deficit and hence high government borrowing combined with economic recovery. That has placed pressures on the price of money, which has driven up interest rates in the United States. In those circumstances, operating in a free money market between Canada and the United States or between Europe and the United States, money flows from Canada or from western Europe into the United States, seeking higher returns. In those circumstances, Canada or, indeed, Germany this past week, has one of two options. It can either let interest rates move upward in response to the situation in the United States, or allow the value of the Canadian dollar to reduce.
The Bank of Canada has been acting to moderate fluctuations, but the principal challenge-
Enough!

-facing Canadian economic management and the management of European economies or, indeed, of any industrialized countries, is the situation in the United States where interest rates have been increasing.

subtopic: STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE-CANADA AND UNITED STATES UNEMPLOYMENT RATES
STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE-CANADA AND UNITED STATES UNEMPLOYMENT RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I direct my question to the Minister of State for Finance. The
Minister undoubtedly has witnessed Iona and the Seven Dwarfs proceeding to their leadership convention. He has undoubtedly noted that certain of the dwarfs have made statements. For example, the Minister of Justice, sometimes referred to as "Sleepy" has stated, and I quote:
We all know, basically, how to stimulate the economy to create employment.
Would the Minister indicate to the House if he has consulted with the Minister of Justice, who apparently has the answers?
Second, would he indicate to the House, in relation to the American reference which he has just made, why its unemployment rate is at 7.8 per cent while ours is at a level which results in 442,000 more Canadians being out of work in this country compared to the number which would be out of work if we had the same rate of unemployment as there is in the United States?

subtopic: STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE-CANADA AND UNITED STATES UNEMPLOYMENT RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer to the Hon. Member's first question is no. The answer to the second question is that we have been creating jobs in Canada at a rate faster than in the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE-CANADA AND UNITED STATES UNEMPLOYMENT RATES
STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF JUSTICE-CANADA AND UNITED STATES UNEMPLOYMENT RATES
speechtext: The fact is, as the Member should know, during the past year we have created jobs at a record level. Equally we have seen a growth in our labour force which has exceeded that of almost any other industrialized country. In other words, as fast as we have been creating additional jobs more people have joined the work force. The basic fact is that government policies, whether direct government support for job creation or policies intended to encourage private sector job creation, have been successful in creating jobs at record rates.

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister indicate why Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and Switzerland have an interest rate structure no higher than 8 per cent at a time when we have to live with 12 per cent and rising? In addition, if he has not consulted with the Minister of Justice, would he indicate whether he has consulted one of the other dwarfs, Bashful, sometimes referred to as John Turner, to find out why he seeded the mess in the period from 1972 to 1976, which the Government has now inherited?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should recognize that the prime rate in Canada has been running at one half a percentage point
May 10, 1984

below that of the United States. We have maintained in past months a substantial difference in the prime rate between our two countries. The Hon. Member refers to Germany. If he looked at the facts he would see that the German Central Bank in recent weeks has recognized that interest rates in Germany will probably have to increase in response to the situation in the U.S.
There is a broadly based concern throughout the OECD member countries about U.S. interest rate policies. But that concern is not limited only to those member states; it also exists in the United States itself. The chairman of the Federal Reserve system has expressed serious concern about the Government's deficit management and the fact that interest rates are going up. That situation affects all countries in the world. The Hon. Member should recognize that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of State for Finance and relates to the effect escalating interest rates are having on the housing industry and jobs. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member may recall that the Minister of Finance on several occasions has indicated to the House that the mortgage interest rate protection plan will be introduced in the House shortly. However, he said, it would be necessary to consult with the construction industry, the mortgage money industry, consumers, and a range of interested institutions about the details of the program. As I said, the Minister of Finance indicated on several occasions that we shall introduce the necessary legislation shortly.

Mr. Speaker, consultations with those industries will lead to their annihilation because there will be no private sector left. With 15 per cent and 16 per cent mortgage rates, Mr. Speaker, they cannot sell homes, and there will be no industry.

subtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I would like to direct my question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. He will have become aware in the last few minutes that the central bank rate has gone up more than half a percentage point and is now in excess of 11.5 per cent. Six month T-Bills are up to 12.5 per cent, which means that the prime rate in Canada will be going up in the next few days for home owners, farmers, small businessmen and the like.
This trend line has been demonstrated for the last number of weeks, yet the Minister of Finance keeps telling us that there is nothing he can really do, that he is basically a financial eunuch and he has to look to Paul Volker in the United States for guidance. Will the Prime Minister of Canada tell us today whether he agrees that there is nothing the Minister of Finance of the Government of Canada can do to keep interest rates from continuing to increase?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not agree with the phraseology of the Hon. Member. He refers to changes in interest rates today and yesterday. If he referred to the answers just given by the Minister of State for Finance he would see that the question was dealt with very competently. What Hon. Members opposite seem to forget is that, in order to borrow money at a reasonably low interest rate, you have to find lenders who are prepared to lend their money at a low interest rate. That means Canadian savers who want to lend money at a rate substantially less than they can get across the border in New York. I do not know many lenders who will, out of a spirit of nationalism, lend their money to Canadians at a rate lower than they can get in the United States. This is not blaming our plight on the United States. It is just stating an obvious economic fact of international financial marketing.
Currencies from all over the world have been flowing to the U.S., including Canadian currency, for the past few years since the Americans have had very high interest rates. That is

May 10, 1984
Oral Questions
why the Canadian dollar, the Deutschemark, the yen, all currencies, including the very strong ones, have fallen against the American dollar. Incidentally, the Canadian dollar has fallen less than all those other currencies. That is not too complicated, Mr. Speaker.
From the point of view of the borrowers, everyone would like to borrow at a lower interest rate, but you have to find lenders who are prepared to lend at a lower interest rate. Until the NDP or the Tory Party can give us a pool of such lenders who are prepared to lend at rates below the market, then we will sort of be bound by market rates.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF BANK ACT TO PROVIDE LOWER INTEREST RATE SPREAD
REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF BANK ACT TO PROVIDE LOWER INTEREST RATE SPREAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, reports which we have received over the last number of months have indicated one of the reasons interest rates are high to the consumers of Canada, whether one is seeking a mortgage, a small business loan or a farm loan from the chartered banks particularly is that the differential between what the banks are charging and what they are giving their depositors is larger than it has ever been in Canadian history. That is because the Bank Act provides for that.
The Government has indicated a real interest in opening up the Bank Act to assist the foreign banks. This would be a breaking of precedent of its 10 year rule. If the Government is going to ask us to open the Bank Act to assist foreign banks operating in Canada, does the Prime Minister not feel it would be appropriate to amend the Bank Act to provide a lower interest rate spread so that Canadian consumers would receive some benefit?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF BANK ACT TO PROVIDE LOWER INTEREST RATE SPREAD

our position on interest rates. I would like to inform the Prime Minister of Canada that we feel it is now time to take an independent position. A ceiling of $100,000 or even $500,000 could be provided so that 99.9 per cent of Canadians would not be adversely impacted.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member can vent his spleen as much as he wants against Paul Volker. I carry no brief for Mr. Volker's monetary policies or, for that matter, for those of the administration. In point of fact the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and myself have taken issue with the United States on their high interest rates. We have indicated that they have various consequences, not only on Canada but on investments throughout the developing world.
We can always criticize Mr. Volker, but I notice that the Hon. Member conveniently side-stepped my earlier point that until he has supplied us with a pool of Canadian savers who are prepared to lend at a rate lower than the American rate, we cannot force them to lend their savings at a lower rate.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for small business. The highest level of potential job creation exists within the small business sector. Likewise, the largest number of jobs are lost in small business when high interest rates are allowed to continue to rise as they have risen again today. ly in the role of small business in pulling the country into a period of economic recovery. That was the main emphasis of the February 15 Budget. those who happen to live in our six largest cities, will be eligible for lower and discount fares, and guaranteed service of any kind?

Oh, oh!

speechtext: With that sense of humour you could have been leader.

Mr. Speaker, I have already put two questions in 30 seconds.

Member, what we said in January was that we intended to have a new policy in place this spring that would provide the framework within which the private sector and the airline industry could begin making the kinds of management decisions and choices that would lead to lower air

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Pension Act is supposed to operate on the case law principle. speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: CASE LAW-REQUEST FOR ACCEPTANCE OF PRECEDENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that particular matter within the medical profession is an issue on which there are varied opinions. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald:
That this House profoundly regrets the two-year delay of the Government in bringing in promised legislation to improve guaranteed income supplements for low-income single elderly Canadians, and condemns the Government for its failure to respond to the innovative proposals of the all-party Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform to expand opportunities for Canadians under age 65 to make adequate provision for income in their retirement years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me more than a little pleasure to rise today to discuss the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I must confess that I wondered if the Hon. Member was truly being serious in making this proposal. It seems that the Hon. Member is concerned with the Government's failure to respond to the innovative proposals of the all-Party task force on pension reform.
Hon. Members are aware of, and applaud, the work of the task force of which the Hon. Member was a part. We must go back and look at the contents of this report. Either the Hon. Member has forgotten what was proposed by the task force she belonged to or she was not around when the Budget was brought down on February 15. The Government has listened very closely to the task force and has indicated in no uncertain terms that it is its intention to act as expeditiously as possible to bring the wide range of much needed pension reforms into existence.
Where's the beef?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Hon. Members will recall that the parliamentary task force was appointed to do some very serious and difficult things within a limited time frame. They were called upon to report on the proposal made by the Government in its green paper Better Pensions for Canadians and particularly to look at inflation protection under private plans, proposals for the Quebec and Canada Pension Plans, survivor benefits, expansion of mandatory pension arrangements by public or private plans, Canada Pension Plan financing and the special pension problems facing women. They were given until the end of 1983 to make their report and they did so well within that time period.
The Government brought forward a detailed and positive response in the February Budget. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands is concerned that this is not going to be brought into legislation. To say her concern is not well founded is an understatement. The GIS is due to increase by $25 on July 1 and by another $25 on December 1. To say that this will be done without legislation being presented is quite improbable, to say the least.

It can't be.
May 10, 1984

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That is right, so the legislation will be brought in. That is exactly what we are saying. It is a finance Bill.
Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the Government has finance Bills that it wants to bring forward. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) says we have to pass the Western Grain Stabilization Act, that we have to help farmers. I do not find any fault with that. That is quite commendable. In fact, it is a priority item.
The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) brought up the same question. He was told by the Prime Minister that we on this side of the House have many priorities on what we have to put forward, some of which are finance Bills, one of which is the increase in the GIS.
The Opposition has to make up its mind. It cannot have it both ways. It cannot come down 100 per cent in wanting to help the prairie farmers on the one hand, and then the next day say that we immediately have to throw the concerns of the prairie farmers aside and now present to the House the concerns of our elderly and poor. Either one-half of the Conservative Party is not talking to the other half, or they have the shortest memories that this House has ever witnessed.
This morning we heard from the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer). He says that what is being done with the Bills, certainly the green paper Better Pensions for Canadians and the task force report, does not reflect the Minister's ideas. If Members opposite had not held this Opposition Day when the Minister was out of the country, she would be able to present her ideas and clarify them.
The Minister's ideas certainly do not need any clarification. The Minister and the Government have been very supportive of what was brought down by the task force on pension reform. This debate is completely unnecessary. It is pure schizophrenia on the part of the Opposition. It indicates that they do not know what their priorities are, not only from year to year, month to month, week to week, but from day to day.
What was it that the task force proposed? It made 65 separate recommendations. I do not intend to go into all 65- there is a sigh of relief and that is in order-but let us look at some of them in terms of the original mandate.
First, on inflation problems, under employer-sponsored plans the task force proposed to drop the excess interest approach and instead proposed that all future pension accruals be updated on the Consumer Price Index less 2.5 per cent, subject to two limits. One was based on a portfolio of investment return and the other was based on an economic indicator which the Chief Statistician proposes eventually to develop.
The Government has responded positively to this proposal. The February 15 Budget indicated that the Government agreed to move from the excess earnings approach and instead would propose inflation protection based on 60 per cent of the Consumer Price Index. This is very similar to the task force proposal, although it is simpler and at current inflation rates would be somewhat more generous.
Supply
Second, on survivor benefits in the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans, the task force recommended that survivor benefits not be terminated on remarriage, that survivor benefits after 65 be set at 30 per cent rather than 60 per cent of the deceased spouse's pension, and that the divorced spouses be given the survivor's pension. Again, the Government has indicated its intention to act.
The Budget stated that legislation will be brought forward providing there is sufficient provincial consent to ensure that survivor benefits will be continued on remarriage. I certainly hope that the provinces will give their consent to such a provision, and I would urge all Members to use their good offices with provincial governments to support this proposal.
On the other proposals that are of a more controversial nature, I am sure that the task force members were aware of the federal-provincial nature of the Canada Pension Plan. Major CPP benefits can only be made with provincial consent. Accordingly, the Government has proposed to place further changes to CPP survivor benefits on the agenda for federal-provincial discussion.
Third, the task force recommended that no immediate action be taken on mandatory pension arrangements. The federal Government has gone along with this recommendation for now but has announced through the Budget broad measures to encourage expansion of voluntary pension coverage for full-time and part-time workers. As well, the federal Government will continue to monitor these coverage items.
Dealing with the other specific topics of CPP funding and homemakers' pensions, which again are matters requiring provincial agreement, the federal Government has agreed to enter into federal-provincial discussions and is sure that the task force's ideas will be given serious consideration by the provinces. Of course, this by no means covers the full extent of the task force recommendations nor does it cover the extent of the actions proposed by the federal Government, far from it. Indeed, even the immediate steps that the federal Government has taken have gone beyond those recommended by the task force.
For example, dealing with pension vesting and portability, the undertaking contained in the Budget for the vesting of pensions after two years of plan membership and for the portability of pensions through the transfer of built-up credits is almost identical to the task force proposal. The Budget undertaking regarding sexual equality and the provision of annuities is again virtually the same as that proposed by the task force. There should be equal pensions for male and female employees retiring under equal circumstances.
The Government has also agreed with the task force on the need to move forward with protection for spouses through the provision of pension rights for survivors of private plan contributions. It also agreed to the need for access, on marriage breakdown, to the private pension credits which have been built up through the efforts of both spouses during the marriage.

May 10, 1984
Supply
Dealing with plan termination insurance, the Budget agrees with the indication of the task force that this is not required at this time.
Dealing with tax assistance for retirement saving, the Budget announced what amounts to the most sweeping changes ever made in this area which will give equivalent access to tax assistance regardless of the vehicle used. It will also set comprehensive lifetime limits on contributions and index the limits on contributions and pensions annually. That was definitely the thrust of the task force report.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that although I applaud the Government for having taken this kind of action so soon after the task force report, I applaud even more the Government's generous approach which will encourage Canadians to put more money toward retirement, and indeed to put even more money toward retirement than the task force recommended. I also applaud the Government for its decision to increase spending on the guaranteed income supplement to which I referred earlier.
The increase of $460 million a year that the Government is giving to single pensioners and couples composed of only one pensioner is greater than the increase of $350 million that the task force recommended. Although the increase of $50 per month is not as large as the increase of $102 per month that some pensioners would have received under the task force's proposal, the coverage of the Government's increase is much broader. I am sure that all Members will agree that pensioners need and deserve this help at this time.
I am also pleased that the Government decided to act immediately to help immigrant pensioners who are in need by guaranteeing them the same pension as is now guaranteed to lifelong residents of Canada through Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement, rather than undertaking the further study which was proposed by the task force.
The actions to be taken that were announced in the federal Budget cannot all take place at one time and cannot cure all of the problems of the public and private pension systems. For one thing, the broad provincial jurisdiction in this area must be acknowledged. It is the provinces which must set the pension standards for 90 per cent of Canadians, which must approve the Canada Pension Plan changes and which provide extra top-ups to the federal guaranteed income supplement. These things must be taken into consideration. Nevertheless, even if we consider only the immediate steps to be taken by the federal Government, we must see that the consensus of the task force has been translated into action.
We will be seeing legislative action to amend the Old Age Security Act to provide needed help for low-income singles, for families struggling to get by on a single pension and for immigrants who come to Canada late in life. We will see amendments to the Canada Pension Plan to extend the creditsharing provisions so that spouses of CPP contributors will be able to claim a personal CPP pension as a right either on marriage breakdown or at age 65. We will be seeing federal pension benefit standards for inflation protection, portable pensions, vesting, disclosure, survivor benefits and a sharing of
pension rights by spouses. We will be seeing fairer tax rules and the creation of new tax vehicles so that small business employers can have their own pension fund. All this is clearly in keeping with the principles underlying the task force proposals and indeed in most cases is practically indentical in detail to those principles.
It is certain that not all of those 65 recommendations will be implemented in the first phase. We hope to see even more accomplished in the second phase, with the co-operation of course of both levels of government. However, to suggest that the federal Government has not acted, and acted boldly, to implement these innovative ideas is to both misunderstand the Budget and to belittle some of the important recommendations of the parliamentary task force. I would say to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands that I do not understand her motion and that I feel the Government has acted very directly in this very important field.

Mr. Speaker, I never thought that I would see the day when a Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare would stand in the House and say, as the Hon. Member did, that to date the concerns of the elderly poor in the country were, in his words, completely unnecessary. Not only did I think that I would never hear a Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister say that but I thought I would never hear a Member from Cape Breton-The Sydneys say that. The predecessor of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys made it a point on his own to raise in the House the concerns of the elderly time after time. I know many people from Cape Breton-The Sydneys who are over the age of 65, who are in need and who are waiting to hear when this legislation which was promised last February will be brought forward.
The Hon. Member has said that today's debate is completely unnecessary. Since he thinks that the debate as to when this legislation is coming forward is completely unnecessary, I would like to ask him if he would tell us the date on which this legislation will be introduced into the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, there may be a question as to whether or not she heard me correctly. I do not know whether she has a need for remedial hearing techniques or not. However, Mr. Speaker, I certainly did not say that the concerns of the aged are unnecessary and I certainly did not say that all of their problems have been corrected. I did say that I do not feel, as seems to be suggested by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, that the Government has done nothing with respect to the task force report and that the Government is insensitive to the needs of pensioners. In fact, I said that the Budget addressed a great many of the concerns of the aged.
The Hon. Member refers to my constituency of Cape Breton-The Sydneys. I would remind the former Member from this constituency of the unemployment which exists in this
May 10, 1984

area of approximately 35 per cent in real terms. There are young couples of whom neither of the spouses has a job and who are without the funds necessary to meet the needs of their children. There are young people who cannot get their first job. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was on this task force, Mr. Speaker. I am sure she realizes that one of the criteria we considered was that not all of the money which the Government had available to help Canadians would be used for the benefit of people over the age of 65. There are other needs which have to be considered. While there are real needs of people over the age of 65, these needs must be weighed in conjunction with the needs generally in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He spent a fair bit of time showing that the Government in fact had responded positively to the recommendations of the pension reform task force. Could he indicate to us which one of those proposals, which he highlighted as being proposals on which the Government is moving, will see legislative form before the next federal election?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) for his question. As the Government House Leader said today, this is a question being negotiated by the House Leaders and as such is part of their discussions. I must say, however, that there is a great deal of concern on this side of the House with the plight of those over the age of 65 who are living below the poverty level. I do not doubt the sincerity of the Hon. Member for Provencher and of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands when they speak about the plight of these people. This question certainly should be addressed as soon as possible. With that I agree. However, I do feel that the Parties have to get together. Hon. Members on the other side must determine how they want it to go. We hear on one day that we have to deal immediately with the plight of the farmers in the west, and we hear on another day that we must deal immediately with those people over the age of 65. Those questions are very important, but unless we get the proper consensus of all Parties working together, these questions are not going to be resolved as soon as we would like.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question. Obviously, one of the things with which the task force was concerned was fairness and pension reform. In view of the fact that the $50 per month increase in the GIS amounts to $1.61 a day for most pensioners on full GIS, and in view of the fact that in the budget papers there was a proposal to permit those workers making up to $86,000 to deduct up to $15,000 a year in pension contributions-which was against the recommendations of the task force, as the Hon. Member knows-would the Hon. Member indicate whether he feels that that is fair? A single pensioner on GIS would receive $50 a month, and an individual making up to $86,000 may claim up to $7,500 off his taxes. Is that fair?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) that the

priority is with those who are living under the poverty level. Regardless of what the Budget says, the priority will be given to that group of people.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question for the Parliamentary Secretary. The motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) talks about pension reform. However, I believe all Hon. Members should be aware that when Parliament passed Bill C-139, the effect of that particular Bill was that workmen's compensation would now be included for the purposes of calculating the guaranteed income supplement. I have a number of constituents, Mr. Speaker, who have received substantial reductions in the incomes which they were previously receiving.
I wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary has received representations from various people across the country and whether he has received representations from Hon. Members opposite as well as from those in our own Party to try to have this particular piece of legislation changed so that it can go back to the way it was, which is, that workmen's compensation would not be included for the purposes of the guaranteed income supplement.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one further point. Those who receive guaranteed income supplements in my province are entitled to other benefits, for instance, in terms of medical care, drugs, and property taxes. Now that workmen's compensation has been added to their total income, that has been wiped out. In addition, they have received a reduction in their over-all income, so instead of having a 20 per cent reduction, it amounts to approximately 40 per cent. I wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary, who I know has been working very diligently on pension reform for the last number of years, has had that type of representation in the last number of months?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, (Mr. Dingwall), I would tell him that I have, like he has himself, received representations regarding this question. It comes down to a matter of dealing with funds which are available. Certainly, it is not an easy task when you consider that people over the age of 65 are not receiving the amount of funding which they should receive and which we would like them to receive.
The question is how best to utilize the funds which can be made available. I, like the Hon. Member, have made representations requesting that perhaps people over the age of 65 should not have their compensation payments included for tax purposes. The rationale which has been explained is that when people are under the age of 65, certainly they are at a disadvantage. Over the age of 65 it is difficult for most people to do the things they once did. That is not to say that we would not want to see that funding remain with those over the age of 65, and the matter is being reviewed and possibly will be changed. However, it relates to a question of funding needs in this country and how these needs generally must be met, not

Mr. Speaker, coming from my constituency, I need not tell the House what an interest my constituents have in the old age supplement and in Bills such as those projected by the Government. I am sorry that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is not in her place today. I understand that she is in Belgium attempting to come to an agreement with that country over an exchange of pensions. I would be much comforted if I thought she might bring back the same attitude which that government has toward payment of pensions to women at age 60. The Belgian Government does it in a very simple way, whereas the Canadian Government prefers to put in place the most disorderly hodge-podge of regulations which anyone could imagine determining how much money it will disburse to senior citizens who are female.
Today's debate is brought about because of the Budget which came down on February 15. At that time, as reported on page 1430 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) had this to say in his Budget speech:
In the Throne Speech, the Government made a commitment to introduce legislation to increase the GIS for single pensioners. My colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, will soon be introducing legislation to increase the maximum payment to this group of pensioners by $50 a month.
Of course, it was going to come in two phases some five months apart, if it was to come at all. The Minister also stated:
Provision will also be made to see that persons receiving partial old age pension, most of whom are Canadian immigrants, have Guaranteed Income Supplement benefits sufficient to give them the same minimum income as other pensioners.
The legislation which is now due comes about because of the parliamentary task force which recommended pension reform. Its recommendations were quite progressive and comprehensive. I felt rather sorry for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacLellan) who had to stand up and claim that the Budget declaration of the Minister of Finance represented the wishes of the task force. There is a kind of Tiny Tim and Ebenezer Scrooge comparison which can be made between the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister of Finance in this dialogue which may or may not be going on.
It is not that we are quarrelling with the Bills we think are going to come about, but it is a real possibility that these Bills will not be passed before the summer break. Parliamentary Secretaries and the Government House Leader all tell us that, yes, they are urgent, yet we never see the Bills. Surely it is misleading the House to have Government representatives talk about early passage of these Bills when they have not yet been put on the Order Paper. There are 34 days left to us, including several Opposition Days. We granted another day today to the Liberals to take that rag-tag bunch of candidates they have,
sort out the six worst of them and keep the other one. I would just as soon see them draw lots; we might end up with a better candidate.
There is one of them here right now.

I am sure he feels the same way. That would give him an increased chance.
If the Government was to bring the GIS Bill forward, I am sure there would be no prolonged debate. Then we can get to the Bill, which this Government seems to consider so very important, respecting the Crown corporations which the Liberals have fostered throughout their period in office. They can then guarantee that certain people will be appointed to these positions before they indulge in the deluge of an election we are going to have.
One of the problems we have in trying to discuss this Bill is that we are very short on details and we have not yet seen the Bill. When we speak to Ministers who will be responsible for this legislation, we find that they do not seem to know what is going to be in the Bill. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) answered the many questions put to him concerning war veterans's allowances, but he is not able to tell us what he is going to do.
All our problems in this area started with the 1977 amendment to the Old Age Security Act. It established stricter qualifications for old age security and it established the provision of partial pensions for immigrants. I opposed that measure at the time, pointing out that it was going to be an administrative nightmare, and now I am not happy that my forecast came true. The amendment was predicated on the idea that all other nations were going to have reciprocal agreements with Canada, but they have not done so. That was the underlying assumption when the Government decided that a partial pension would be feasible. The result has been a kind of guaranteed poverty class. We allow people into Canada who are too old to get in sufficient pension time before they reach 65 so as to have a decent living from the OAS and GIS.
I would like to speak for a moment now about the British pensioners, of whom there are 40,000 resident in Canada at the present time. They have been waiting for years for reciprocal pensions. In 1978, in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that pension reciprocity with Britain was her number one priority. Well, last October, the Minister answered a question in the House in part by saying that the dossier of the reciprocal agreement for pensions and other social programs between Great Britain and Canada is an active one. This March she put out a statement in which she said that she regrets to advise that, in spite of Canada's efforts, the British Government has decided not to proceed at this time with the social security agreement. This is devastating news, and I think we should have an opportunity to ask how it came about. Is it simply that the Minister is unable to get along with the British, or is it that the British really do not want to pay these pensions? It seems only just that a person who paid into
May 10, 1984

a pension fund should be able to get money out. This situation has left a great number of British pensioners in the lurch.
Another group of people who are suffering badly are the immigrants from Third World countries. It is impossible to have reciprocal agreements with some of those countries because they do not have a pension system in effect. We bring people in on the assumption that we will give them a partial pension and they are supposed to get a pension from their home country. Consequently, these people end up at pensionable age with about a quarter of a pension, if they have been here for ten years, out of the possible 40 year period for building up pension credits.
This problem was brought to the attention of the task force by a variety of witnesses. The main point they made was that these people were not only unable to get a partial pension from their homeland, but they are frequently not employed in an occupation in Canada which has either a private pension plan or a Canada Pension Plan. This of course leaves them destitute at a time when most Canadians expect to retire at the age of 65 and live on their OAS and GIS.
In 1977, the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, now the Minister of Finance, stated that those unable to qualify for adequate OAS and GIS pensions had the option of going on welfare. That surely is not a satisfactory answer with regard to what we are going to do with the people who came into this country in good faith and now find they will not be like other Canadians when they reach 65 and receive the OAS and the GIS. Instead, according to the present Minister of Finance, they will be expected to go on welfare.
We now find that the same Minister has introduced a Budget which promised to increase the GIS to those receiving partial OAS in order to ensure that they have the same minimum income as other pensioners. This will require an increase to the GIS so that that portion will be over 100 per cent. As everyone is aware, the old age security is paid at a basic rate without any means test. The guaranteed income supplement is also paid up to a certain rate given in dollars. If you only have a quarter of half the rate of the old age security, plus a full guaranteed income supplement, you are still at a lower level than what is thought to be the poverty level, or indeed the sustenance level for Canadians. As is typical of the Liberal Government, it is now going to bring in more legislation which will attempt to address the grievous fault caused by its last amendment to the Old Age Security Act.
It would be much simpler, Mr. Speaker, to abolish the system of partial entitlement to the old age security and allow immigrants to qualify for full old age security after 10 years, as they did before the amendment was brought in. We should provide them with the same guaranteed income supplement as is received by all Canadian pensioners, subject to the same requirement of an income test. I do not see the value in going around a three-sided triangle by changing perfectly good old age security provisions, making room for partial pensions, and then devising another piece of legislation to cater to some of
Supply
the people who cannot get the sustenance level which would be caused by the first piece of legislation. Surely it would have been simpler to cancel the amendment to the legislation which was introduced in 1977. I am rather proud of having opposed that amendment at the time.
Let us look at the war veterans allowance. Possibly to the surprise of many, and apparently to the surprise of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the war veterans allowance is correlated with the guaranteed income supplement. When the guaranteed income supplement increases, the war veterans allowance increases. There is a small Department of Veterans Affairs top-up procedure which takes place. The war veterans allowance is added to, so that the person drawing this allowance will always be a little better off than those who are not veterans.
On March 14 I asked the Minister a question in the House of Commons. I was seeking clarification as to whether veterans under 65 who receive war veterans allowance would benefit from the announced increase in the guaranteed income supplement. I was trying to determine whether this would apply to those recipients who are considered to be single for the purposes of WVA or to all recipients of WVA, married and single. In response to my question, the Minister stated:
I can assure the Hon. Member that the provisions which were included in the Budget to provide for a $25 increase in the GIS as of July 1, and a further $25 increase as of December 1, will be passed through to all veterans simply by increasing the ceiling.
This was obviously nonsense. The Minister did not understand what the Minister of Finance had said in his Budget and did not realize the complexity of it. Therefore, he was unable to make clear which veterans would benefit from the increase. I gave him an opportunity to clarify this, but he did not seem to be able to do so.
These matters have been brought up in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs on four separate occasions. In a statement to the committee on March 20, the Minister indicated that the increase in GIS to single recipients would be reflected in an increase in war veterans allowance for single recipients. This, of course, would ignore the married recipients who are over 65. They would find themselves falling back to the same level as the single recipients. Since then, the deputy minister has been unable to explain precisely how the increase will be put into effect. He has further confused the issue and then promised members of the committee that the Minister would clarify matters shortly. As yet we have had no statement from the Minister on this subject. When he was speaking to the House this morning in this Opposition Day debate, I noticed that he did not clarify the subject.
Obviously, some very technical changes will have to be made to the war veterans allowance. If the Bills come before Parliament and are passed, the Minister of Veterans Affairs will be expected to decree by how much each category of the war veterans allowance will go up. I suspect that the Minister still does not know what is going to be in these Bills when they are presented. This is part of the difficulty we are having. It seems only reasonable to me that the Minister should at least have the notification before the Bills are produced. He had better be

May 10, 1984
Supply
ready for them because he should be writing the regulations at the present time to ensure that the War Veterans Allowance Act is amended or changed by regulation, which he is entitled to do, to comply with these forthcoming Bills.
I have listened to Members on both sides of the House saying whose fault it is that these Bills have not been presented. Clearly, this side wants to have the Bill on the guaranteed income supplement as early as possible. We want the grain stabilization Bill as well. The Government has promised to deliver both these Bills. We want them. I expect they will pass fairly quickly. Then the Government can debate, as long as it wants, the Bill on how to handle its Crown corporations. I see no reason to continue with this procrastination. A large segment of the population of Canada is liable to be hurt if the Bill I referred to is not brought in in time to be passed before the end of the session at the end of June. It is outrageous that on February 15 they should have made statements in the Budget which have not as yet been acted upon. I am reluctantly coming to the conclusion that the Government is planning not to pass those Bills and to try to fight an election campaign saying that it is someone else's fault that the Bills have not been passed. I expect that trick would easily be seen through. I look forward to hearing someone who has some responsibility on the Government side tell us when the Government proposes not only to put these Bills on the Order Paper but to table them for first reading.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak, if I may, for a few moments with regard to the motion which is before us in terms of the reform of pensions. Earlier in my comments I mentioned workmen's compensation being calculated in for the purpose of the guaranteed income supplement. The effect of Bill C-139 is-

Would the Hon. Member not concur with me that when workmen's compensation is calculated into GIS and war veterans allowance is excluded for the purposes of GIS, that is somewhat unfair and discriminatory? We can probably find all sorts of cases in which veterans are certainly more deserving than those receiving workmen's compensation. Alternatively, would the Member not concur with me that there are perhaps very many situations where individuals who are in receipt of workmen's compensation are perhaps, in some
instances, more deserving of that income than some veterans? I would not advocate that as a general principle. However, with regard to pension reform, various sections of the Income Tax Act have been amended. They have indiscriminately inflicted a dire consequence on senior citizens.
On many occasions the Hon. Member has stood in his place and advocated better pension reform not only for veterans but for the elderly. I would like the Hon. Member to concur with me in order that we could take joint action, not in a partisan, political way, but in an effective way, to have the Minister for National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) address this very important issue.
As l have heard the Hon. Member himself say on several occasions, we do not want to act indiscriminately against those in need. I believe that by calculating workmen's compensation into the guaranteed income supplement we are not only reducing the incomes of numerous constituents on the list I have before me, we are in fact penalizing them twice. I would hope that the Hon. Member, whom I have respected since my entry into this Chamber, would concur with my desire to right a wrong which I believe to be in Bill C-139. However, I need his help and I am wondering if he is prepared to give it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his complimentary remarks. The Government frequently introduces legislation apparently with no idea as to its side effects. Perhaps it is because there are not enough Members from Cape Breton who understand the lives that the working people lead and the misfortunes they suffer. Having said that, I do not see the possibility of my ever saying that veterans are being treated too generously, particularly by that Government.
I agree with the Hon. Member's point about workmen's compensation. I suggest that it is outrageous and typical of the Government to want to reduce their guaranteed income supplement, because they are being paid for an injury they suffered in the work place under a program for which they pay normal taxes. Everyone else pays workmen's compensation fees. I commend the Hon. Member for his attitude. I am sorry that it is not shared by Members on the front benches.

I have one further comment. I concur with the substance of the Hon. Member's remarks, but I want the record to be clear that the effects of Bill C-139 were not seen in this Chamber when it was introduced. It took several months not only for the bureaucracy but for those affected by the legislation to comprehend it fully. I do not think there was any desire, politically or otherwise, to affect those in greatest need. I believe there must be a consensus among Members of Parliament, who, on the one hand, stand in the Chamber to say that they are concerned about the elderly and, on the other hand, pass a law that is very unjust.
I need the assistance both of Members opposite and of Members on this side of the House to bring this matter to the
May 10, 1984

attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) as well as of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLar-en).
The sections of the Income Tax Act that are involved are Section 81, Section 56 and Section 110. They must be repealed before this wrong can be corrected. I need the assistance of Members opposite, and I hope that at the end of the day, when the debate has been concluded, no one will interpret my suggestion as being in any way partisan, because I think we are all concerned about those senior citizens who are in the greatest of need. Some of them have had a substantial reduction, ranging from $50 to in excess of $200 a month.
I want to thank the Hon. Member, whom I have respected and admired since my entry into this Chamber, for his assistance in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that the Hon. Member and I are members from different committees. My interest is in the Department of Veterans Affairs and in senior citizens. The problem he is raising concerns the work place and workmen's compensation.
I do not know how much pressure he can exert on the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but certainly we on this side are forever lining up to try to put questions to the Hon. Minister. I find it difficult on many days to find her in the House early in Question Period. I do not like to say that, but it seems to be the case.
Certainly we will try our best, as far as I am concerned, to assist the Hon. Member, who I think has brought to light a very good point. It indicates a reform in the pension system that is needed and one that was pointed out so clearly in the task force report. With the exception of a couple of measures that we are still waiting to see in print in the House, it has been totally ignored by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence I would like to give one example of the dire straits in which some people in this country find themselves. I refer to a 70-year old gentleman by the name of Malcolm Woodland who lives in the town of New Waterford. Prior to Bill C-139, his income was $336.38.
Per month?

Per month. However, the effect of the legislation is to reduce that income to $266.28. It does not allow him to take advantage of the social programs that the Government of Nova Scotia has put into place in terms of his property taxes and moneys that are made available for drugs.
It is inconceivable that senior bureaucrats, of whatever politi- cal affiliation, should have put that provision into the legislation. As politicians, we are allowing that wrong to continue. I want to give the House judicial notice that it has not heard the end of this. I have petitions coming from the towns of Glace Bay, New Waterford and Sydney Mines. I will

That being said, I still think the day is wasted, but I shall go on just the same. I want to quote today's Opposition motion and correct a mistake in what it says:
That this House profoundly regrets the two-year delay of the Government in bringing in promised legislation to improve Guaranteed Income Supplements for low-income single elderly Canadians-
It is not two years but two months. Let me explain the obvious: In 1981 we held the National Conference; in 1982 we tabled the Green Paper, and in December 1983 we tabled the Report of the Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform.
Well, if I count from December 1983 to-and if I take the date on which the Budget was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), that is only two months. I think the Government did very well to engage in consultations. We are responsible people, and we therefore had to consult with the other parties concerned. Once again, I want to give senior citizens in this country the assurance that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will keep her word, as always.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that in his Budget speech, the Minister of Finance announced that the Government intended to pursue pension reform in two stages. During the first stage, the Government proposes to increase the guaranteed income supplement, to improve minimum standards for private pension plans, to strengthen the Canada Pension Plan and improve the benefits to women, and also to improve tax assistance for retirement saving. These measures, set forth in the February Budget of this year, were meant to improve substantially the pension situation of both today's pensioners and of Canadians who will retire in the future. However, the Government realizes that although the measures
are very important, further steps must be taken. That is why a second stage is planned which will start this summer and will include discussions and especially negotiations with the provinces on a series of further proposals.
After the consultation process, we shall now proceed with the second stage, namely, negotiations. I think that if the Members Opposite were sitting on this side of the House, they would do the same.
I was favourably impressed with the spirit of co-operation shown by Ontario in this respect. The proposals for reform by the Government of Ontario augur well for federal-provincial discussions of pension reform.
Of the major issues that will be on the agenda during federal-provincial discussions, I would like to mention four: first, the homemaker pension; second, improving disability benefits; third, greater flexibility in the age of entitlement; and fourth, financing of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. All of this depends on federal-provincial negotiations, Mr. Speaker.
All proposals were the subject of studies and recommendations by the Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform. The Government realizes, however, that the issues are complex and require further study and further discussion with the provinces.
Take, for instance, the issue of homemaker pensions. It is a complex issue and a number of solutions have been suggested. The pension proposal was made for various reasons: to recognize the value of work done by women in the home; to meet the need for adequate retirement income; to provide for greater financial autonomy and to recognize the contribution of each individual to the marriage union. All of these reasons are entirely valid, and I cannot agree more. Proposals for changes made during the first stage of pension reform also support this initiative. In addition, it was suggested that an additional pension based on wage equivalent as well as compulsory contributions be made a part of the Canada Pension Plan. A proposal like this one raises a number of questions, however.
First, what price is set on the work of women in the home? Is half the average industrial wage a valid and fair assessment? If so, how can we justify this? Who is going to pay for the pension? Will this be the full responsibility of the family breadwinner? Should low-wage earners be subsidized by all working Canadians? If the family breadwinner is to pay, does that settle the problem of women's financial dependence? And are we to differentiate between women who work full time in the home and those who combine a job outside the home with housework? Does work done in the home by certain individuals make them eligible for a pension, while women who have a job outside the home are not eligible?
May 10, 1984

I am raising these questions, not because I am against pensions for women, on the contrary! I simply wish to draw your attention to the complex issues that must be resolved before we can reach a consensus on the subject.
Changes to the Canada Pension Plan require the approval of two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the population. Because of the many aspects of this question, the Government has decided to postpone the question of including a pension for housewives in the Canada Pension Plan until the second stage of consultations with the provinces. I may add that the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans are very similar, and that the federal Government and the provinces, including Quebec, are very anxious to maintain the parallels between the two plans. It would be unthinkable to make important changes in the Canada Pension Plan without prior consultation with Quebec and without ensuring that the parallels between the two plans are maintained.
The second major issue on the agenda for discussion with the provinces is the ban on more flexible rules on eligibility for benefits, especially the Old Age Security benefits and retirement benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. The Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform had to admit that lowering the age of entitlement for the Old Age Security pension should be examined more closely.
The financial implications are quite considerable. For instance, there is the impact on the labour force participation rate. Many programs already exist for this age group, such as provincial social assistance programs, and disability benefits under the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. We must consider the implications for all these programs.
The Government of Ontario has already announced it would support the addition of an early retirement plan to the Canada Pension Plan which would be similar to the one introduced under the Quebec Pension Plan. Mr. Speaker, as of January 1984, all senior citizens in Quebec are eligible for pension benefits under the Quebec Pension Plan when they are 60 years old. Considering that the Government of Ontario looks favourably on this measure, the outlook for reaching an agreement with the other provinces is promising. However, we must have a comprehensive policy for all pre-retirement measures, and to achieve this, further study and consultation at the federal and provincial levels will be necessary.
A third important item on the agenda for our discussions with the Provinces is the question of disability benefits. The Hon. Monique Begin has already embarked on a major consultation process with the Provinces in this regard. She has made proposals to improve disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. Improving these benefits would mean bringing them up to the level of the benefits paid to a pensioner aged 65 or over who receives the old age security pension as well as retirement benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. The maximum disability pension now represents only about 57

per cent of this amount. I remember, Mr. Speaker, how important this question of disability pensions was when I sat on the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped and I realize that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been negotiating ever since. She has been negotiating with the Provinces for the past two years. I note that this is the third item on the agenda for federal-provincial discussions. Work is going on, but everything cannot be done overnight. I was impatientmyself when I saw that nothing much was being done to follow-up on the recommendations of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. Most Provinces have indicated their agreement in principle with this proposal, on the understanding that some arrangement can be reached on the funding of the Canada Pension Plan. This question is also on the agenda for the second stage of the pension reform. On the other hand, the Hon. Monique Begin and her colleagues have embarked on a major federal-provincial study to examine the possibility of introducing a comprehensive disability insurance plan designed to solve the problems of those who are not protected by existing federal and provincial programs or whose coverage is inadequate.
This study is now under way and should continue for some time yet, unfortunately. However, before it can be introduced, such a plan calls for comprehensive studies, and the federal and provincial ministers have agreed to continue to improve existing plans until they receive the recommendations to be made by this federal-provincial committee, which has not submitted its report yet. In view of the general agreement in principle on this issue, we can expect the second stage of pension reform to be successful in this regard.

Indeed, contributions to the CPP should increase from 3.6 per cent of insurable earnings to about 6 per cent by the end of this century. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer) said this morning. I hope I did not hear him correctly. I hope the Canadian people did not understand that the system was jeopardized because it is not. We could carry on as we are doing now for another 20 years without increasing the 3.6 per cent rate of contributions by a single cent. I will go on, but I want to reassure the public by saying that there is nothing to fear, as did the NDP Member who worked with us on this matter, the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) who also reassured the public this morning by saying that there was no need to worry about it. There are now several options for funding the Canada Pension Plan. In principle,

The Minister of Finance said that he planned to co-operate with the provinces in order to set a proper schedule of contributions, with special attention being paid to the proposal of the task force which suggested a pay-as-you-go formula taking into account any improvement in allowances. It is clear that the government is taking its responsibilities not only as far as the financing of the Canada Pension Plan is concerned but also with respect to the proposals made by the parliamentary task force. However, it is quite obvious that one of the basic questions to be solved is the lack of protection made available to Canadians. Less than half of all Canadians have an adequate pension plan. Should governments extend the scope of compulsory pension plans to solve the problem? It is important to give the private sector as many opportunities as possible to show that it can provide an adequate pension to retired Canadians.
All the steps taken should encourage the private sector and provide the necessary tools to perform that task. The government intends to monitor the response of parties concerned. Our committee suggested a three-year period to enable the private sector to take charge. We also suggested that after that period, if the private sector has not taken its responsibilities and borne its own share of the employees' pension plan, the government should perhaps double the Canada Pension Plan or find other alternatives.
I think that the government has shown that it was ready to move quickly in the area of pension reform. It has also shown some responsibility and caution concerning the more complex issues to be dealt with in the second phase of pension reform. The provincial governments have also a capital role to play. The extent and quality of pension reform will very much depend on the outcome of negotiations. Nevertheless, I am confident that we will succeed in thoroughly altering the pension system in the shortest possible time in the interests and for the welfare of all Canadian men and women.
